newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean occupiers quit Australian embassy.
newsitem.headline: Chilean occupiers quit Australian embassy.

text.p: Four Chilean women who occupied the Australian embassy to demand better treatment for jailed guerrillas left the embassy as peacefully as they arrived on Thursday after pleas from the Chilean government.

The four women, all relatives of leftist rebels who call themselves political prisoners, walked out of the embassy after a seven-hour sit-in to call attention to their demands for better prison conditions.

"It was all thoroughly peaceful. It was never a siege at any stage," said Australian Ambassador Ken Berry. "We're quite prepared to listen to their story, but entering and then refusing to leave an embassy is not the proper way to be heard."

The four women walked into the embassy's section like any other tourists hoping to travel to Australia and, once inside, refused to leave and unfurled a banner demanding "justice for the political prisoners."

They said they were on a hunger strike, shouted slogans to reporters and read a statement through a megaphone from behind the fence of the elegant, French-style embassy in a wealthy Santiago neighbourhood.
The embassy staff refused to talk to them or give them water and closed the building.

Representatives of the women met away from the embassy with Chile's Deputy Interior Secretary Belisario Velasco, who said the women had made their point and persuaded them to leave the embassy, Velasco told reporters.
Neither the embassy nor the government apparently ever considered using force to dislodge the women.
"These people have come just to make a point," said one embassy official.

All four said they were relatives of left-wing guerrillas in two Santiago jails, including the maximum security prison where four guerrillas escaped last month with the help of a helicopter piloted by their comrades.

The relatives demanded the government lift a ban on prison visits and relax tight restrictions on outdoor time for the inmates, measures imposed after the spectacular Dec. 30 prison break. About 50 prisoners inside the maximum security jail are on a hunger strike to protest the crackdown.
The peacefulness of the embassy episode provoked joking references to the tense siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru by guerrillas demanding freedom for their jailed comrades.

"We were about to decide what demands we would make to let them out," said an embassy employee. Reporters jokingly shouted to the women that they had made a mistake and that the Japanese mission was a few blocks away.
Authorities gave no immediate reason why the strikers chose to occupy the Australian rather than another embassy.
